origin: Great Basin and Intermountain West — interior BC south to Oregon, east to Montana, Wyoming and western Colorado
habitat: Dry plains, mountain slopes and sandy washes on lean rocky ground
blurb: The tall cousin of our native scarlet globemallow: open wands of grey-felted stems hung with apricot-orange cups from late spring into summer, growing out of a taproot that shrugs off heat, lean soil and drought. A magnet for the specialist globemallow bees.
water: Low; xeric — no supplemental water once established
spread: Clumping from a taproot; self-sows into bare ground
seasons: Apricot-orange cups May–July, often reblooming after rain; grey-green scalloped foliage; dies back to the crown in winter
wildlife: Special value to native bees, including the globemallow specialist bees

care.hardiness: Rated for USDA zones 4–9, so cold is a non-issue at Boulder's zone 5b–6a. It is a Great Basin plant of dry plains and mountain slopes, which is to say it is built for the same heat, wind and thin soil the Front Range delivers.[2][1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost or in early fall, into lean, sharply drained ground. It grows from a taproot, so set out young plants rather than trying to move established ones. In a container use a deep pot and a gritty mineral mix, and keep it on the dry side — a rich, moisture-retentive potting mix is the fastest way to rot the crown.[2][1]
care.sun: Full sun. This is a plant of open dry plains and sunny slopes; in shade it stretches, flops and flowers poorly.[1]
care.soil: Dry, rocky, well-drained soil. It carries a medium tolerance for calcium carbonate, so our alkaline Front Range clay-loams suit it as long as drainage is sharp — amend heavy clay with grit rather than compost.[1][2]
care.water: Low water use, and genuinely xeric once the taproot is down. The USDA guide places it squarely in waterwise western landscaping; overwatering, not drought, is what kills it here.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space 18–24 in apart. Plants are open and branching rather than dense, so a group of three reads better than a single specimen.[2]
care.propagation: By seed. Like the rest of the genus it has an impermeable seed coat that acts as a physical dormancy mechanism, blocking water uptake — so untreated seed germinates poorly and erratically. It also self-sows into open ground once established.[2][1]
care.sow: Scarify the seed — the USDA guide is explicit that the impermeable coat should be broken with boiling water or another treatment before planting if you want decent germination. Their trials reached about 87% germination with scarification, rising to the low 90s with scarification plus a 24-hour water soak. Without breaking that coat, expect very little.[2]
care.bloom: Orange to apricot-pink cups, roughly May through July, carried along the upper stems. Deadheading spent wands often brings a second flush in a wet late summer.[1][2]
care.maintenance: Very low. Cut the dead stems back to the crown in late winter or early spring. Skip the fertilizer and skip the compost — lean soil keeps it upright, while rich soil makes it lanky and short-lived.[2][3]
care.selfsow: It self-sows into bare, disturbed ground — useful in a xeric planting, easy to pull where you don't want it. Hoe seedlings off young or deadhead before the capsules dry if you'd rather it stayed put.[2][1]
care.troubles: Few problems in a dry, sunny, well-drained site; crown and root rot in wet or heavy ground is the main failure. Like other globemallows the whole plant is covered in fine star-shaped hairs that can irritate skin and eyes — wear gloves and don't rub your eyes when cutting it back or collecting seed.[2][1]

edible.summary: No documented culinary use; grown as a xeric ornamental, and the star-shaped leaf hairs are a skin and eye irritant.[1][2]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for Munro's globemallow, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. The practical hazard is mechanical, not chemical: like our native scarlet globemallow, the plant is coated in fine stellate (star-shaped) hairs that irritate skin and especially eyes — the reason globemallows carry folk names like 'sore-eye poppy'. Wear gloves when cutting it back or collecting seed, and keep your hands away from your eyes.[1][2]
